title: SpaceX’s Earnings Show Elon Wiped Out Two-Thirds Of Twitter’s Ad Business
text:
Failures

When SpaceX filed for its IPO, we went through the S-1 to point out just how far off the mark Elon Musk’s predictions about his Twitter takeover turned out to be. Indeed, the failure of Twitter as a business was so catastrophic, Musk had to hide it by merging all his Xs together: he had xAI buy X (formerly Twitter), and then had SpaceX buy xAI. But when Musk was buying Twitter and needed investors, he made bold promises about how he would succeed — promises the media and his investors treated as perfectly reasonable. He said he would take Twitter’s ad revenue from $4.5 billion in 2021 to $12 billion in 2027 (and then also many more billions in subscription revenue).

Now that SpaceX is a public company, he has to report some of that revenue, though it’s all merged and buried in footnotes. But there’s enough info in there to show that advertising revenue is way, way below what it was when he took over the site. And it’s shrinking.

In the 10-Q, all of X’s revenue is now (misleadingly) labeled “AI” revenue, but even then the reporting has to admit ad revenue took a big hit, dropping $160 million compared to the first half of 2025 (which was already way, way, way lower than when Elon took over the site), going from $870 million in 2025 to $710 million in the first half of 2026. The company tries to claim that this decrease in ad revenue is because they “transitioned to a new advertising platform which impacted ad sales for a short period of time.” Which is a curious explanation, given that on the analyst call, CFO Bret Johnsen credited that very same “overhauled” ad-tech platform for the very slight quarter-over-quarter uptick in ad revenue. The same overhaul apparently both tanked the business and rescued it, depending on which direction the number was moving.

And even the claim that the overhaul increased ad revenue is suspicious given that if you compare the 2nd quarter from last year to this year… ad revenue dropped from $426 million to $367 million, year over year. Some overhaul.

I kinda think that if your transition to a new ad platform decreases ad sales by $160 million, someone fucked up badly somewhere. Especially when it’s a nearly 20% year-over-year drop.

Let’s break all this down: In the second quarter of 2022, the last full quarter before Elon took over, Twitter brought in $1.08 billion in ad revenue. In the second quarter of 2026, X brought in $367 million. That’s $713 million a quarter, gone. Elon has wiped out two-thirds of Twitter’s ad business over the exact period in which he promised investors he’d nearly triple it.

And it’s not for lack of trying. Over the past year X has made a ton of experiments and revamps to improve the experience (though the main person in charge of all that, just left). I’d argue that the company was just rebuilding all of the stuff Elon killed after first taking over the company, but none of it has brought advertisers back.

Turns out that telling advertisers to go fuck themselves… and then suing other advertisers for not advertising… doesn’t make anyone want to advertise with you.

Still, it seems like someone should be pointing out how far off the mark Elon has been. He promised twelve billion dollars in ad revenue within the next year. That’s three billion a quarter. X just did $367 million — about an eighth of the pace, and shrinking. You can talk all you want about his rockets and robots, he’s not magically going to grow ad revenue 700% in the next 18 months.

So, tell me again how Elon is a business genius?

Filed Under: advertising revenue, elon musk, revenue
	

	Companies: spacex, twitter, x, xai

To be fair to Elon (I never thought of doing so), two-thirds of Twitter users are certainly bots (even if he “fixed it” just as he “fixed” CSAM the first weeks if bought Twitter) and advertisers are well aware of that.
But he also has promised that his $44B toy would one day be a $1T company, and he’s certainly not wrong about this given the SpaceX market share trajectory.

So, tell me again how Elon is a business genius?

Because, like Trump, he banked on his father’s wealth, and only has his own bluster about his value and those without sense only see that.

Also he got to keep his shares in Paypal after they fired him. Letting him fall upwards.

Also, since the business world equates money to success, whoever gets the most money via business must, by definition, be a genius at business.

This terminology sometimes leaks outside of the business world, and we should be careful to avoid that. But, linguistic nitpicking aside, society in general is set up to make people want money—and to drive corporations toward that goal in a psychopathic way, per the 2003 film “The Corporation”.

For the uninitiated, “genius” and “wealthy son of an apartheid emerald mine owner” look a lot alike.

It’s not about making money.  It was never about making money.  Please stop thinking like a stereotypical capitalist-American.  Elon Musk did not buy Twitter to make money.

The purpose of having lots of money is to spend it.  For a benevolent example, which I will then contrast directly to Elon Musk’s sheer malevolence, this blurb from the Gates Foundation is absolutely true (2022-11/2023-09; boldface added):

While hormonal contraceptives have allowed generations of women to plan their families, they aren’t right for everyone. Side effects such as unpredictable uterine bleeding, mood changes, and headaches can be annoying at best and in the worst cases debilitating. Nearly all of the products on the market involve hormones, so women are faced with a terrible choice: Endure the side effects? Or risk unintended and unwanted pregnancy?

Developing other options for those women makes sense, but historically investments in nonhormonal contraceptives have been nearly nonexistent.

That’s spending money through a nonprofit foundation, to make the world a better place.  It’s not to make money.  Money is power, and power can be wielded for good.

I’m an old-school Micro$oft-hater, still angry at the Halloween documents.  I have no Windows in my house!  —Suddenly, I love Bill Gates.

In contrast, this extweet from Elon Musk on a platform he owns is medical misinformation—all the more pernicious because it’s a half-truth subtly mixed with bullshit, wildly exaggerated, then restated in absolute terms (2024-02-16):

Hormonal birth control makes you fat, doubles risk of depression & triples risk of suicide. This is the clear scientific consensus, but very few people seem to know it.

https://x.com/elonmusk/status/1758569518442701250

At this juncture, I reminder you that in 2024, Elon Musk spent out of pocket a quarter-billion dollars to re-install Donald Trump.  Musk’s expense on election interference is second only to whatever Russian taxpayer money Putin must have spent in 2016.  Musk has the budget of a state-level threat actor.

ExTwitter costed much more than that to buy, and it costs money to run.  Musk merely needs to keep it afloat somehow.  He has as a tool in his hand one of the most powerful mass-propaganda platforms in the modern world.  He doesn’t need it to make a profit.  He doesn’t even need it to break even.  He just needs to keep it non-bankrupt—somehow—such as by bilking SpaceX investors, who are ipso facto easy to fool.

Money is power, if and only if you’re so cheerful about spending it.

———

I pick the foregoing example for personal reasons.  For decades, I’ve had a vision for a nonhormonal contraceptive, a pet idea about it, a realistic dream—but I’m neither a billionaire nor a biomedical researcher.  Many years before the Gates Foundation took this up, it was on my personal shortlist of things I’d do if I were a billionaire or a biomedical researcher.

It’s totally doable!  It just needs lots of money, and lots of time for biomedical researchers to spend that money.  Expect for practical results to be at least 10–20 years out.  “The best time to plant a tree is twenty years ago…”

I have no power to make it happen.  The Gates Foundation can make it happen.  I wish I were a billionaire.  I’m smart and ruthless.  Why the fuck didn’t I make “be a billionaire!” a goal when I was young?  Bill Gates co-founded “Micro Soft” when he was 19 years old.

Historically, hormonal contraceptive R&D was brought to fruition by a wealthy heiress, Katharine McCormick, whom Margaret Sanger persuaded to spend the fucking money.  From her share of the McCormick family fortune, Katherine McCormick dumped millions of dollars into a visionary project that a pharmaceutical company had already terminated as unprofitable.  It would not have happened otherwise.

By hook or by crook, Elon Musk wants to make every person with a uterus bear zillions of babies to overpopulate a world that he’s actively turning into a global shithole.  It’s partly because Musk is an addled drug addict, endued with a quasi-religious belief that “AI” will solve all problems—and anyway, after we’ve finished ruining Earth, we can just move to Mars.  (Or some lucky subset of “we”.)  It’s only partly because he’s an asshole.

Not all of Musk’s dreams are realistic, but he can definitely succeed at his dream of making the world a worse place.  He just needs to spend the money.
